annotations.text: The weapon readout, redrawn five ways. The corner is the one readout a pilot reads without looking away from their own hull: a row per trigger wearing its loadout, a row per charge with its count, growing up out of the bottom-left safe corner. Every board keeps what earlier rounds settled: the marks themselves (shared with the touch pads, one drawing per weapon), the rung ramp carried by the round's own hue, no labels, no bounty. What changes is the ground under the rows and what a count looks like. One loadout on every board so they compare: gun at rung 2 with spray and bounce, bomb at rung 1 with prox and shrapnel, two of three repels, one of two bursts. Everything is drawn from palette.lua and marks.lua geometry at z = 2, the size a large monitor actually reaches.

As shipped. A row is its mark and the counts are loose dots. Nothing says the four rows are one instrument, nothing under them says where the corner begins, and a spent charge is a hollow dot three points across. The marks are not the problem: they took several rounds of care already and no board here redraws them.

A - The rail. One spine out of a chamfered foot in the corner, and every row visibly hangs off it: a nub per row reaching to where its mark begins, a tick per row seam, the top fading out past the last row. Counts become chamfered magazine cells, so a spent charge keeps its outline and the row never changes width. The rounds read as leaving a rack rather than floating. The cheapest direction to build (a dozen segments and the cells) and the most house: this HUD already speaks in hairline rules and chamfers. Cost: the spine is chrome that says nothing on its own, and on a bare kit two rows wear a fair amount of rail (board beside).
The rail on a fresh spawn, which is most of the corner's life: two plain rows, no charges yet. The spine keeps the corner reading as one instrument even when the kit is empty.

B - Bays. A chamfered lip per row, the bracket the radar and the expanded map already wear, and one hairline deck under the block. Each weapon sits in its own bay, which answers where a row begins better than a shared spine can, and gives hover an obvious hit shape. Cells for counts as on A. Cost: five brackets where the rail spends one line, and a lip this small flirts with reading as a parenthesis.

C - The hull plan. The corner is your ship, drawn faint in panel ink, and each mark hangs off the hardpoint that fires it by a hairline leader: the gun at the nose because that is where it is, the bomb in the keel, charges racked off the wing. The most fiction of the five and the best answer to what this corner is about, the machine you are flying. The costs are real: twice the height of the stack, a hardpoint table per hull, and the leaders put ink between you and the counts.

D - The fire arc. A quarter instrument swung out of the corner itself: two arcs, ticks every ten degrees, a station per row, the dial corner answered from diagonally opposite. The most cockpit of the five. Cost: a curved layout for row-shaped content. Hover cards, row order and the direction the block grows in all get harder, and it spends the most screen on the same four facts.

E - Live fire. The shipped geometry, unmoved, but the corner answers the one question a fight actually asks it: can I press this now. A fired trigger recoils with a flash and goes dim, then the barrel relights from the tail as the cooldown runs out, so the line itself is the gauge. A ready row breathes on the clock DEPLOY and ON AIR already breathe on. The last charge pulses. fire_cooldown already sits in sim_ship (sim.h), so this costs one small core getter plus draw code, and it composes with any of A through D rather than competing with them. The strip along the top is one row's life drawn out flat.
